Other options that have been tried include interferon alfa and tamoxifen.1,3-5,11 Despite some initial positive data for tamoxifen, large randomised clinical trials failed to show any survival benefit for therapy at conventional doses,14,15 and meta-analyses13,16 confirmed this. Adoptive immuno- therapy, using activated T-cells cultured with interleukin-2 and a monoclonal anti-CD3 antibody, has been reported to lower recurrence after resection.17 Trials of octreotide have produced conflicting results.4 In contrast to the poor response of hepatocellular carcino- ma to therapy, better progress has been made in strategies for its prevention. Neonatal vaccination against hepatitis B has dramatically decreased the incidence of chronic in- fection in children in Taiwan, and reduced the incidence of hepatocellular carcinoma. This may be a more promising approach in areas where the disease is common.2 There is evidence that interferon alfa can delay or prevent the de- velopment of hepatocellular carcinoma in cirrhotic pa- tients with hepatitis C infection.18 Chemoprevention may also be a useful approach after surgical resection: use of a synthetic retinoid, peretinoin, was found to reduce the de- velopment of second primary tumours after resection.19,20 The liver is the most common site of metastatic disease.21 For most malignancies the presence of liver metastases is indicative of generalised dissemination, but isolated meta- static liver disease is common in colorectal cancer (p.665) and rarer cancers such as some neuroendocrine tumours (see Carcinoid Tumours, above). In contrast to disseminat- ed disease, treatment of such isolated liver metastases can prolong survival. Surgical resection is the preferred treat- ment if feasible. Palliative or cytoreductive surgery is ben- eficial in hepatic metastases from neuroendocrine tumours because of their slow growth.21 Combined resection and adjuvant chemotherapy (hepatic arterial or systemic) is un- der investigation for colorectal liver metastases.
